note: Vol. I No. 19. THE 1 APRIL LETTER LIST IS PRINTED AGAIN HERE, in the same two cut columns of page 3, and it is NOT minted again: the cohort was minted from 1834-04-01, and c001 and c002 below mint ONLY the sixteen names this printing carries that the first printing's OCR crushed. One list makes one cohort of people (T-0299, and the rule T-0292 set for the October list, which was printed three times). This issue's own contribution is the town rather than the list: the spring building season opening, a soap and candle manufactory, and the block of storefronts on South Water Street that page 4 column 3 reads more cleanly than any other column in the month — Peter Cohen's store, the boot and shoe shop next door to it, and Philo Carpenter's drugs. Sixteen of thirty-two segmenter columns carry the Tesseract fallback banner, and page 4's eight all do.

claims.notes: A REPRINT, RECORDED AND ALMOST ENTIRELY UNMINTED. The heading here reads `List of` then `EMAINIG in the P` then `IM. on the first day` — the same 1 April 1834 Chicago list the previous week printed, run a second time as the post office of the period ran its lists for two or three weeks. T-0292 settled what to do with a list printed more than once: mint it ONCE, from the witness that carries it whole, and record the other printings without minting their names, so one list makes one cohort. NEITHER PRINTING CARRIES IT WHOLE, which is the wrinkle here. This column reads distinctly cleaner than 1834-04-01's for A-J — it is what settles `Robt. V. Allen`, `Maria S. Arnold` and `Oscar L. Hawley` in that issue's normalized reading — and it carries eleven names that the first printing's lines lost to the interleaved editorial. Those eleven are minted HERE, once, and nothing else in this column is. `lines_of_claim` names only the heading and the eleven lines those names stand on, so the quote is not the whole list a second time.

claims.notes: THE SPRING BUILDING SEASON OPENING, in the editor's own words and dated to the week before 8 April 1834. It is the first of two such notices in this month — 1834-04-16 counts `seven or eight buildings` raised in one week — and together they say that the town's fabric in the spring of 1834 was being added to at something like a building every day of good weather. The line the count would be on, 2200, is debris the transcription itself flags `[uncertain: baildings tie erir]`, so NO NUMBER IS READ HERE; the number belongs to the 1834-04-16 claim, which has one. `The mechanic` is the building trades, and the sentence is quoted rather than paraphrased because its subject is exactly who was at work.

claims.notes: A MANUFACTORY IS A BUILDING WITH A PROCESS IN IT, and this one is new in April 1834 — `have commenced`. No address is printed, so the placement is `none`; a soap and candle works is the kind of neighbour a town puts at its edge and this one's site is simply not stated. The same Daniel Elston fitted up a smoke house earlier in the year (1834-04-01 c007), so the house runs two rendering trades by the spring. The dateline gives `April` and no day; the copy date is the first of the month by convention.

claims.notes: THE ANCHOR THE REST OF THE BLOCK IS MEASURED FROM. Peter Cohen on South Water Street is the worked fixture of this whole corpus (T-0257, from the scene-date issue of 1835-07-01) and here he is fifteen months earlier, in the same street, with the same trade widened to clothing. What makes the store placeable at all is the NEXT advertisement in this column (c007), which is placed against it.

The proprietors are not minted: the firm name is cut to `E & co.` and `(WNE & CO.` in every April column that carries it, and P. The trade is NOT stated anywhere in the surviving half and is not guessed at. The dateline `March 4, 1834` is the notice's own and is a week before the dissolution it reports, which is how these notices ran — the copy was set for the first insertion and the date of dissolution is inside the text.
